title: Saint Stephen (26 December)
hook: the first martyr the day after Christmas: the crib and the cross together

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nativity, and John's gospel with no manger at all. Your line was the word made flesh. What bodily kindness did you manage? Day six hundred forty-one.

December 26. The wrapping paper is in bags by the curb, there are leftovers in every container in the house, and the tree is still lit. If you go to Mass that morning, the priest is wearing red. Red, the color of blood. On the first day after Christmas, the Church remembers a man who was stoned to death for his faith. It can feel like whiplash, from lullabies to a martyrdom in a single night. The Church put it there on purpose.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER.` → `THE PRIEST WEARS RED.` → `FROM LULLABY TO MARTYR.`

segments.voice: Stephen first appears in Acts 6, in a dispute about food. The early community in Jerusalem was feeding its widows, and the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked. So the apostles chose seven men to serve at tables, and the first named is Stephen, full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. He was, in Catholic tradition, one of the first deacons. He also preached, with a power his opponents couldn't answer, and he was brought before the council. In Acts 7 he gives a long speech retelling Israel's story, from Abraham to Moses to the temple, and it ends badly. An angry crowd drags him outside the city and stones him. As the stones fall he prays: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then, on his knees: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Close echoes of two things Jesus says on the cross in Luke's gospel, now on the lips of one of his followers. And Luke adds a detail that matters later: the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul. The word martyr comes from the Greek for witness. Stephen's own name, stephanos, means a crown, the wreath given to a winner. So why the day after Christmas? Because the Church refuses to let the crib stay sweet. The child in the manger grows up to be crucified, and people who follow him have sometimes paid with their lives. The crib and the cross belong in the same picture. And the carol Good King Wenceslas is set on the feast of Stephen too: a king going out in the snow to help a poor man gathering fuel.
screen: `A DISPUTE ABOUT FOOD.` · `STONED, AND PRAYING FOR THEM.` · `SAUL HOLDS THE COATS.` · `MARTYR MEANS WITNESS.` · then, large: `LORD, LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a kindness for the poor. Stephen's first job was making sure widows got fed. Sit and bring to mind someone in need you could actually help this week: a food bank, a neighbor short on money, a person you pass on the same corner every day. Choose one concrete thing, and when. Then sit with Stephen's harder prayer, for the people who hurt him. If you pray, you can pray for someone who has wronged you. If you don't, simply hold them without wishing them harm. The bell holds the time.
Saint Stephen. One of the seven chosen in Jerusalem, honored by tradition as the first Christian martyr, remembered on December 26 in red. Today's word.
Your line: the crib and the cross. Today, do your kindness for someone poor, and keep the sweetness of Christmas honest. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics keep December 26 as the feast of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, with red vestments inside the Christmas octave; in some countries it is also a day of giving to the poor.

fork.setup: you're Stephen. the stones are falling and you're on your knees. what are your last words?

a prayer that their sin not be held against them.
a demand for a fair trial.

original.note: Greek: a crown or victor's wreath; Stephen's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: December 26 is just the day after Christmas.
what it means: the feast of Stephen, the first martyr, set right after the birth so the crib and the cross stay together.
what a scholar hears: Acts 7 has his last words echo Luke 23:34 and 46; martys means witness, stephanos a crown, and Saul enters the story at his feet.

sources.quoted: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.

notes: Verse numbering of Stephen's last words differs between Douay-Rheims and KJV by one verse; confirm.
The seven in Acts 6 are traditionally regarded as the first deacons, though Acts does not use the noun 'deacon' for them. Script says 'in Catholic tradition'.
'Good King Wenceslas' (J. M. Neale, 1853) mentioned as an old carol set on the feast of Stephen; confirm.
Careful framing: Stephen's death attributed to 'an angry crowd' after a hearing before the council, avoiding collective blame.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Acts does not call Stephen young; his words are now 'close echoes' of Luke 23, not 'the same'; the Wenceslas sentence no longer claims a false causal link; 'first martyr' framed as tradition.
